subject: [RFC PATCH 0/7] cgroup: charge kernel work to the cgroup it is done for

reviews.author: Tejun Heo
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach of moving a kworker into the target cgroup before running it has scalability issues due to contention on cgroup_mutex and cgroup_threadgroup_rwsem, and suggested an alternative direction for remote charging where a kthread explicitly specifies which cgroup the work is intended for.

Reviewer noted that the proposed solution does not address net rx, another major source of displaced CPU usage, and suggested adopting an approach that can cover both memory reclaim and net rx use cases by counting per-cgroup received packets and prorating CPU consumption.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concern about the unconditional forgiveness of debt capping, suggesting instead that the cgroup should be slowed down to throttle new work generation and avoid out-of-control situations, similar to IO control mechanisms.
reviews.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 11:47:04AM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

This doesn't translate to net rx, which is another major source of
displaced CPU usage. Switching membership on each packet isn't going to
work there. Attribution can't happen that way. We'd much rather count
per-cgroup received packets and prorate the CPU consumption. If at all
possible, I think it'd be better to adopt an approach which can cover
both use cases.

---

I don't like the debt capping. Having debt doesn't have to mean that
the cgroup doesn't get any bandwidth at all. The cgroup just needs to
be slowed down enough that the generation of new work is throttled and
the whole thing doesn't go out of control. IO control already does
this: when IO debt is accumulated, userspace is heavily throttled, but
not completely stalled, until the whole cgroup's consumption comes
under control. I don't see why the debts would need to be forgiven
unconditionally. The cgroup can keep paying them while running at a
minimal rate to avoid triggering stall failures, and if the situation
doesn't resolve quickly, that will most likely trigger pressure based
kills in any reasonable setup anyway.

Thanks.

--
tejun

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledged a concern about accurate accounting of CPU time spent on network receive operations, particularly for modern NICs with dedicated rx queues and old NICs with shared queues. They proposed extending the mechanism to softirqs and considering a special way to account for the latter case, possibly through BPF.

Author agreed to address a concern about CPU time capping and promised to restructure it in the next patch version.
reviews.raw_body:
Very good point. I think we need to think for net rx for two scenarios. First,
the modern NICs with rx steering support and second, old NIC with shared queues.

On the modern NICs where the workloads get their own rx queues, I think the
proposed mechanism can help to do the accurate accounting (I have to extend this
to softirqs as it is limited to kthreads atm) very easily.

The challenge you mentioned is for the old NICs where we get to know the cgroup
assosiation of the rx packets very late (or deep) in the stack. Also CPU spent
on each packet is not necessarily uniform (due to out-of-order or drops or
checksum errors or window shrinking) but for simplicity we can assume uniform
CPU. Maybe the right place to charge for such scenario might be at application
receiving those packets into the memory. I feel like we might need a very
special way to account for this case (maybe through BPF or something). At
the moment to me it seems very hard to have a universal solution which helps
this case and the reclaim case I am targetted.

If you don't mind, I think having solution for modern NICs i.e. dedicated rx
queues, should suffice for now (unless you want the solution for old NICs as
well). Let me know what you think.

---

Sounds good, I will remove this capping in the next version.

Thanks for taking a look.

2026-09-24.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a mechanism to charge kernel work to the cgroup it is being done for, rather than charging it to the root cgroup. This addresses a problem where CPU time spent by kernel threads on behalf of a specific cgroup is not accounted for in that cgroup's statistics and quotas. The approach taken involves allowing kernel threads to specify which cgroup they are working for, and then updating the relevant statistics and quotas accordingly. This will improve resource isolation and accuracy of accounting for CPU usage in various scenarios, including memory reclaim from high-work queues.

reviews.author: Tejun Heo
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the current approach to charging kernel work to a cgroup does not account for CPU time spent in common code for a specific cgroup, and requested remote charging of CPU time similar to IO and memory allocation.

Reviewer Tejun Heo expressed concerns that Rx steering is not suitable for attributing CPU cycles to each cgroup, citing its cumbersome setup and mismatched granularity.

Reviewer suggested combining net rx charging and reclaim CPU charging into a single mechanism where cycles are force-charged to the cgroup after the fact, without involving PSI.
reviews.raw_body:
Hello, Shakeel.

On Thu, Sep 24, 2026 at 02:11:00PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:

---

Rx steering is useful for partitioning the whole machine, but it doesn't
seem like the right tool for attributing CPU cycles to each cgroup. It's
cumbersome to set up and the granularity doesn't match. We aren't going
to be steering net rx processing per cgroup.

---

This doesn't have to be exact or completely synchronous. I don't see why
net rx charging and reclaim CPU charging can't share the same mechanism,
where the cycles are force charged to the cgroup after the fact.

I don't think PSI needs to be involved either. Shared execution in
itself shouldn't create pressure. The forced charge changes the cgroup's
usage, and that usage then creates pressure in the cgroup. IO works the
same way.

Thanks.

--
tejun

reviews.author: Peter Zijlstra
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Peter Zijlstra noted that proxy execution can alleviate the issue, suggesting that tasks waiting on a lock acquisition should contribute to the runnability of the lock holder.

Reviewer Peter Zijlstra strongly disagrees with the patch's approach to charging kernel work to a cgroup, calling it 'horrible garbage' and suggesting that if weight adjustments are needed, using C[23] would be preferable.

Reviewer Peter Zijlstra suggested that instead of moving existing kthreads, new threads should be spawned on cgroup creation and left there, also recommending a less ugly solution to the rmdir issue.
reviews.raw_body:
With proxy execution, this should be alleviated. Then all tasks waiting
on a lock acquisition will contribute to the runnability of the lock
holder.

---

Fiddling with weight sounds like horrible garbage. If you find you need
that, I would really rather you went C[23].

---

You don't move the threads, you spawn them on group creation and leave
them there. I'm sure you can fudge the rmdir thing with less ugly than
you're proposing here and in the other series.

reviews.author: Peter Zijlstra
reviews.summary: Reviewer Peter Zijlstra suggested splitting RX softirqs for each network queue to allow for better resource isolation and priority control, which would enable moving the RX processing threads into specific cgroups.
reviews.raw_body:
Ideally RX would be split for each network queue, rather than lumped
into the one giant softirq that nobody owns.

I know PREEMPT_RT has been wanting something like that for ages. Not all
queues are created equal. Some might want RT priority while others
should definitely not.

Furthermore, without ingress throttling, your RX back charge could
completely deplete the actual cgroup time quota.

Anyway, if you get per queue RX processing threads, then you can move
them into cgroups where so desired.

reviews.author: Sebastian Siewior
reviews.summary: Reviewer suggested modifying softirq flags from per-CPU to per-thread, citing threaded NAPI as an example of a working solution and proposing bulk queues and real-time queues as alternatives.
reviews.raw_body:
What currently kind of works is threaded NAPI. The interrupt wakes the
NAPI thread rather than adding NET_RX to the global flag softirq flags.

I was thinking about making the softirq flags per-thread rather than
per-CPU. This avoid the "catch up" of other raised but unrelated
softirqs.

For now a painless setup is to have "bulk queues" and "real-time" queues
and what gets where is configured via hardware filters.

reviews.author: Shakeel Butt (author)
reviews.summary: Author acknowledged that accurate CPU accounting for net rx in older NICs requires cgroup-aware CPU accounting, agreeing with Peter Zijlstra's feedback.
reviews.raw_body:
For the accurate cpu accounting of net rx, threaded NAPI or softirq is not
that important. I think it is steering packets of the workload/cgroup to their
dedicated queues and only newer NICs have support for hardware rx steering.

For old NICs, we will still be getting packets for different cgroups on the
same NIC queue and I think Tejun is asking for cgroup cpu accounting for this
scenario to work.

reviews.author: Tejun Heo
reviews.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not address the issue of kworkers running in the root cgroup, which results in inaccurate CPU accounting and pressure metrics for the affected cgroups.

Reviewer noted that splitting RX work per queue does not provide sufficient granularity, as there can be many more cgroups than the hardware can support

Tejun Heo noted that if a kthread is handling RX processing for a cgroup, it would share CPU time with other tasks in the cgroup without starving them, and suggested that back-charging can follow a similar principle.

Reviewer Tejun Heo noted that the patch does not address the issue of CPU contention in setups with many cgroups, and requested further consideration to ensure accurate resource isolation.
reviews.raw_body:
Hello, Peter.

On Thu, Oct 01, 2026 at 12:59:09PM +0200, Peter Zijlstra wrote:

---

Rx can be split per queue but the granularity doesn't match. There can be
way more cgroups than the hardware can split queues for.

---

If rx processing slows down, the rx traffic slows down with it. We'd
likely still want to allot some minimum amount of time to non-rx work
while making sure the debt doesn't spiral out of control. If a dedicated
kthread were handling rx for the cgroup, rx would be sharing CPU time with
the rest of the cgroup without choking it completely. The back charging
can follow the same corollary.

---

Same limit here. There are setups with a lot more cgroups than CPUs.

Thanks.

--
tejun
